summary: Lunar Landing Navigator is a free web tool that helps planners choose when and where to land on the Moon. For any lunar site, date and mission length, it shows when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon, ranks the best landing windows, and displays a heatmap of how a one-day or one-degree change affects sunlight. It addresses the challenge by turning orbital geometry into a clear visual decision aid for sunset and Earth set planning. It matters because power, temperature and radio contact all depend on sunlight and Earth visibility, especially near the south pole, where small shifts decide whether a mission succeeds. It also teaches students why lunar mission planning is hard.
details:
What does it do and how does it work? You choose a site (latitude and longitude), a start date, a scan span and a mission length. The app computes Sun and Earth elevation hour by hour using an analytic model of the Moon's orientation, then shows an elevation chart, key statistics (sunlit percentage, longest darkness, next sunset and Earth set), the top 3 landing windows and a sensitivity heatmap. A Moon map marks the site, and a terrain slider sets a horizon angle.

Benefits. It is free, needs no install or account, and runs in any browser, including phones. It makes a hard planning problem easy to see, and it compares dates and sites in seconds.

Intended impact. To help mission planners and students understand how location and date change a lunar mission's feasibility, and to give teams a quick tool for early planning when schedules shift.

Tools and technology. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (canvas charts) for the app, and Python for the engine and tests. I used VS Code, Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting, and NASA Moon imagery (add the exact source).

How is it creative? It puts the decision, not just raw numbers, first. The heatmap shows how fragile a landing window is, and the app gives one ranked answer instead of making users read tables. It also pairs a real NASA Moon map with a polished, space-themed interface.

Factors considered. Sunset and Earth set timing, the Moon's 29.5-day cycle, Earth's libration, terrain blocking the horizon, honest accuracy limits, accessibility on phones, open source credits and clear documentation.
